title: The Book of Consolation Begins: Incurable Wound, Promised Healing
summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to write in a book his words about restoring Israel and Judah. A day of terror is coming, the time of Jacob's distress, but Jacob will be saved out of it; God will break the yoke, raise up David their king, and bring his people home. Zion's wound is incurable by any human remedy, yet the LORD himself will heal it, rebuild the city, and raise a ruler from among them who will draw near to God.
story: After twenty-nine chapters dominated by warning, chapters 30 to 33 are a burst of promise, often called the Book of Consolation. Chapter 29 had told the exiles that God would bring them home after seventy years; these chapters describe what that homecoming will mean. They take up the second half of Jeremiah's call, to build and to plant (1:10). The promises are addressed to both Israel (the northern kingdom, exiled by Assyria over a century earlier) and Judah, so the hope is for the whole people reunited. Chapter 30 lays the foundation: judgment is real and deserved, but it is not God's last word.
historical:
The chapters of the Book of Consolation are not dated individually. Chapter 32 places Jeremiah's purchase of a field in the tenth year of Zedekiah, about 588 or 587 BC, while Babylon besieged Jerusalem, and many scholars think the collection took shape around that time. Some of the poems, especially those addressed to “Jacob,” “Israel,” and Ephraim (the leading northern tribe), may come from Jeremiah's early ministry under Josiah, when that king extended his reforms into the old northern territory after Assyria's decline. Others think the material was gathered and expanded later, during the exile. What is clear is that the hope was spoken into catastrophe. The northern kingdom had been carried off by Assyria after the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, and Judah was about to follow.

The lovers of verse 14 are Judah's former allies, especially Egypt, on whom Judah's kings had relied against Babylon. By the time of the siege it was clear that none of them would help.
cultural:
The images of verses 5 to 7 draw on everyday experience. Childbirth was the ancient world's picture of sudden, unavoidable agony, and the sight of soldiers clutching their stomachs like women in labor would have struck a first reader as both shocking and absurd. The wound imagery of verses 12 to 17 reflects a world with little medicine: a festering wound with no one to treat it was a death sentence. Verse 13 also uses the language of a court case, since no one will plead Zion's cause.

The promises of verses 18 to 20 are concrete. A city rebuilt on her own ruins refers to the tell, the mound built up by generations of settlement, on which ancient cities were rebuilt after destruction. The palace or citadel standing in its rightful place, thanksgiving songs, children, and a congregation before God describe ordinary civic and religious life restored. In verse 21, the ruler who is “one of their own” contrasts with foreign governors, and the idea of drawing near to God was normally a priestly privilege; anyone who approached God's presence uninvited risked death.
literary: Chapter 30 is poetry framed by prose. The prose opening (verses 1 to 4) commands Jeremiah to write, which marks what follows as a record for a future generation. The poems then alternate between distress and deliverance: terror (5 to 7) and freedom (8 and 9), fear and comfort (10 and 11), incurable wound (12 to 15) and healing (16 and 17), ruin and rebuilding (18 to 21). The sharpest turn is between verse 15, where God says he has done these things because of their sins, and verse 17, where he says he will heal their wounds; the same God who wounds is the one who heals. The chapter closes with the covenant formula (verse 22) and then repeats, almost word for word, the storm oracle of 23:19-20, a reminder that restoration does not cancel judgment on the wicked.

outline.t: Write the words in a book
A day of terror: the time of Jacob's distress
The yoke broken; David their king; do not fear, Jacob
The incurable wound that the LORD will heal
The city rebuilt and a ruler who draws near to God

doctrines.note: The chapter holds together an honest account of ruin (the wound is incurable) and an unshaken promise (I will restore your health). Hope rests not on the patient's resources but on the physician.
Verse 22 restates the covenant bond, “And you will be My people, and I will be your God.” Exile had seemed to end it; God promises to renew it, which chapter 31 will develop as a new covenant.

The promise of “David their king, whom I will raise up” (verse 9) looks beyond the historical David, who had died centuries before, to a king of David's line. Verse 21 adds a ruler from their midst who draws near to God.
Even in restoration God disciplines justly (verse 11). His wrath against the wicked and his healing of his people are both expressions of the same purposes of his heart (verse 24).

words.note: Shevut, captivity or fortunes. The phrase shuv shevut, found in verses 3 and 18, can mean either to bring back the captives or to restore the fortunes. Both senses fit: God will reverse the whole situation of exile. The phrase recurs throughout chapters 30 to 33.
Makkah, a blow, wound, or plague. In verses 12 to 17 it names the wound of Judah's judgment, which no one can cure. The same God who struck it promises to heal it (verse 17).

Nagash, to approach or draw near. In verse 21 God brings the ruler near and he approaches God, language usually reserved for priests entering God's presence. The coming leader will have access to God that no one could claim for himself.

christ: Verse 9 speaks of David their king whom God will raise up, a promise shared with Hosea 3:5 and Ezekiel 34:23-24. The New Testament presents Jesus as that son of David, whom God raised up; Zechariah's song speaks of God raising up a horn of salvation in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69). Verse 21, with its ruler who draws near to God, anticipates what the letter to the Hebrews says of Jesus as both king and priest, who has entered God's presence and opened the way for his people to draw near with confidence (Hebrews 4:14-16; 10:19-22). Hebrews does not quote this verse, so the connection is thematic, but it is close. The promise that God will heal an incurable wound finds its deepest Christian expression in the claim that by his wounds we are healed (1 Peter 2:24, drawing on Isaiah 53:5).

hard.q: What is “the time of Jacob's distress,” and is it about the end times?
hard.a: Readers take verse 7 in different ways. Many interpreters, especially in the dispensational tradition, read it as a prophecy of a future period of great tribulation for the Jewish people at the end of the age, followed by national deliverance, connecting it with Daniel 12:1 and Matthew 24:21. Others read it in its historical setting as the catastrophe of the Babylonian conquest and exile, a day without equal for Judah, from which the nation would be saved by the return under Persia; they note that the surrounding verses speak of breaking Babylon's yoke and coming home from captivity. Still others see a pattern in which a historical judgment and deliverance foreshadow a final one. All agree on the chapter's main point: God's people will pass through a day of real anguish, and he will bring them out of it. The details of future events are a second-order question on which faithful readers differ.

questions: God says the wound is incurable and then that he will heal it. Where have you seen something humanly hopeless become the place God worked?
Verse 11 says God will discipline his people justly but not destroy them. How is discipline different from rejection?
The ruler of verse 21 approaches God only because God brings him near. What does that suggest about how anyone comes close to God?
